\section[adelgazar]{adelgazar — to lose weight}

\label{lesson:ES-C503-adelgazar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the joke, then the Spanish for to translate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: adelgazar}
\textbf{adelgazar} — \textquotedblleft{}to lose weight\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quiere adelgazar antes del verano.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He wants to lose weight before the summer.}
\end{quote}

The opposite is \emph{engordar}. It takes \emph{c} before \emph{e}: \emph{adelgacé}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{adelgazar} is \emph{a-}, \emph{delgado}, \textquotedblleft{}thin\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{-azar}: to make thin. \emph{Delgado} is Latin \emph{delicatus}, \textquotedblleft{}delicate\textquotedblright{} — inherited, its \emph{-c-} and \emph{-t-} softened to \emph{-g-} and \emph{-d-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adelgazar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adelgazar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{adelgazar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the joke, then the Spanish for to translate, then say \emph{adelgazar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does adelgazar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To lose weight\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aguantar]{aguantar — to put up with, to bear; to hold}

\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to translate, then the Spanish for to lose weight.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aguantar}
\textbf{aguantar} — \textquotedblleft{}to put up with, to bear; to hold\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I cannot stand the heat.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aguantar} $\leftarrow$ Italian \emph{agguantare}, \textquotedblleft{}to grip, to hold fast\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), built on \emph{guanto}, \textquotedblleft{}a glove\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el esfuerzo}
\textbf{el esfuerzo} — \textquotedblleft{}the effort\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{esfuerzo} is the noun of \emph{esforzarse}, \textquotedblleft{}to strive\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{fuerza}, \textquotedblleft{}strength\textquotedblright{}, from Late Latin \emph{fortia}, from \emph{fortis}, \textquotedblleft{}strong\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[paciente]{paciente — patient}

\label{lesson:ES-C503-paciente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the effort, then the Spanish for the pressure.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: paciente}
\textbf{paciente} — \textquotedblleft{}patient\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay que ser paciente con los niños.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You have to be patient with children.}
\end{quote}

As a noun, \emph{el paciente} or \emph{la paciente} is a patient at a clinic.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{paciente} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{patiens}, \emph{patientem}, \textquotedblleft{}enduring\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), from \emph{pati}, \textquotedblleft{}to suffer\textquotedblright{} — a learned word. A patient person bears things.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}
